title: POLYGAMY IS EVERYWHERE IN PARTS OF THE OLD TESTAMENT—BUT DOES RECORDING IT MEAN GOD APPROVED IT?
paragraphs: POLYGAMY IS EVERYWHERE IN PARTS OF THE OLD TESTAMENT—BUT DOES RECORDING IT MEAN GOD APPROVED IT?

Abraham had more than one woman. Jacob had two wives and two concubines. David had multiple wives. Solomon had hundreds. So why would Christians claim that God’s design for marriage is one man and one woman? The answer is hiding in a distinction we often forget when reading the Bible: Scripture can tell you what happened without telling you to imitate it.
There is a question that can make Christians uncomfortable if they have never seriously wrestled with it.
If God intended marriage to be between one man and one woman…
why is there so much polygamy in the Old Testament?
Among men whose names are woven into the history of God’s people.
Men standing inside the unfolding story that eventually leads to Jesus Christ.
So someone opens the Bible, sees all of this, and asks a question that sounds devastating:
“If God disapproved of polygamy, why did He allow His servants to practice it?”
That question deserves something better than panic.
Because one of the most dangerous mistakes we can make when reading Scripture is assuming that everything the Bible describes is something the Bible prescribes.
That does not make murder holy.
That does not make adultery righteous.
The Bible records deception, incest, drunkenness, idolatry, betrayal, cowardice, sexual immorality, family dysfunction, political corruption, and even the crucifixion of the sinless Son of God.
Recording an event is not the same thing as endorsing it.
Sometimes Scripture shows us human beings exactly as they were because God refuses to build His story upon sanitized biographies.
And that is where this subject becomes much bigger than polygamy.
Because perhaps the scandal you noticed in Abraham, Jacob, David, and Solomon is supposed to make you confront something uncomfortable about yourself:
God has always accomplished His purposes through deeply imperfect people without calling their imperfections good.
Before humanity had accumulated centuries of broken customs and complicated households.
“Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.”
He is joined, clings, holds fast to his wife…
When Jesus was challenged centuries later concerning marriage and divorce, He did not point His listeners toward Solomon’s palace.
He did not say, “Look at what David practiced.”
He did not build His doctrine of marriage upon Jacob’s household.
“Have you not read that he who created them from the beginning made them male and female?”
“Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh.”
“So they are no longer two but one flesh. What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate.”
The Greek expression preserved in Matthew is striking:
Jesus does something enormously important here.
When fallen human practice had complicated marriage, Christ interpreted marriage by returning His hearers to God’s creational intention.
Not merely, “What have human beings done?”
Because if you determine morality simply by finding someone in Scripture who did something, you can make the Bible justify almost anything.
No Christian concludes adultery is therefore righteous.
No Christian concludes drunkenness is therefore God’s ideal.
No Christian concludes denying Christ is acceptable discipleship.
No Christian concludes deception becomes holy because Abraham practiced it.
The existence of sinful or disordered behavior among God’s people does not transform that behavior into God’s design.
And Scripture does not hide the devastation surrounding plural marriages.
Abraham and Sarah received a promise from God, but the waiting became unbearable.
And almost immediately the household began bleeding.
Genesis tells us that when Hagar conceived, relational contempt entered the picture. Sarah became bitter. Hagar suffered. Eventually a mother and child were sent away into the wilderness.
God showed compassion to people caught inside the wreckage.
But divine compassion toward wounded people should never be confused with divine endorsement of every human decision that helped produce the wound.
But through Laban’s deception he received Leah first, then Rachel, and the household expanded further through Bilhah and Zilpah.
It does not read like a romantic advertisement for plural marriage.
Children become entangled in the emotional competition of adults.
Even the naming of children becomes intertwined with longing, pain, rivalry, and the desperate hope of finally being loved.
Sharing a husband with the sister he actually wanted.
Giving birth and wondering whether perhaps this child would finally make her husband love her.
That is not an abstract theological debate.
That is a human heart breaking inside somebody’s home.
The Bible lets you hear it.
Sometimes God does not merely give us a prohibition.
Sometimes Scripture lets us walk through the wreckage.
But his household does not become an advertisement for multiplying them.
A son turning against his father.
If anyone wants to argue that the Old Testament simply celebrates kings collecting wives, Solomon becomes a devastating problem for that argument.
Long before Solomon’s excesses, Deuteronomy 17:17 instructed Israel’s king that he must not multiply wives for himself, lest his heart turn away.
Those words become almost prophetic when you reach Solomon.
The man famous for wisdom ignored a warning already sitting in the Law.
First Kings says Solomon had seven hundred wives of royal birth and three hundred concubines.
Exactly what Deuteronomy warned could happen.
A thousand women did not give Solomon a thousand times more fulfillment.
His multiplied relationships became part of the story of his divided heart.
The man who possessed extraordinary wisdom still discovered that knowing truth is not the same thing as surrendering to truth.
And suddenly Solomon does not feel so ancient anymore.
Maybe not with seven hundred wives.
But we know what God says…
and still convince ourselves that our exception will somehow end differently.
We point toward somebody else who did something similar and survived.
God understands far more than we realize.
But His understanding is not permission to call darkness light.
This is why another distinction matters.
God sometimes regulates realities within a fallen society without presenting those realities as His original ideal.

Biblical laws addressing complicated family situations should therefore be read carefully. A law protecting people within an existing broken social reality does not automatically mean God is declaring every feature of that reality morally ideal.
God cared about people living inside imperfect systems.
The vulnerable could not simply become disposable because powerful men made complicated decisions.
Regulation can restrain evil and protect people without turning every regulated circumstance into the creation ideal.
We see a related principle when Jesus discusses divorce.
When asked why Moses permitted certificates of divorce, Jesus answered that Moses allowed it because of the hardness of human hearts.
Then came the words that should echo through this entire discussion:
“But from the beginning it was not so.”
The difference between what God tolerated within fallen human conditions and what God established in creation.
That is where Jesus takes us.

And Scripture continues developing marriage as covenant faithfulness. Malachi speaks of “the wife of your youth,” describing her as a companion and a wife by covenant, while condemning marital faithlessness.
Then the New Testament takes marriage somewhere even deeper.
Paul writes in Ephesians 5 that marriage mysteriously points beyond itself.
Marriage becomes a living signpost toward covenant love.
Christ does not casually discard His bride.
And suddenly the deepest Christian answer to the question of marriage is not merely a rule.
This is why Christianity cannot build its theology of marriage simply by counting how many wives various Old Testament men possessed.
We must read the entire biblical story.
The Bible is not a collection of disconnected episodes where every character’s behavior carries equal moral authority.
It is the unfolding story of God redeeming sinners and ultimately revealing His saving purposes in Jesus Christ.
And that brings us somewhere unexpectedly personal.
Because perhaps you clicked this expecting an argument about polygamy.
But Scripture has quietly moved the mirror.
You may never have had multiple spouses.
But you have your own chapters you hope nobody reads aloud.
The scandal may have a different name.
A relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
An addiction hidden behind a respectable profile picture.
A marriage quietly dying while everyone online thinks you are happy.
A church face covering a starving soul.
And perhaps you have made the same mistake people sometimes make when reading these Old Testament stories.
You have confused God’s patience with God’s approval.
Therefore you assume everything must be fine.
Therefore perhaps God does not care.
You prayed and still received mercy.
But mercy was never given so we could become comfortable in chains.
Should we continue in sin so grace may increase?
Grace does not rename your chains.
And this is where the scandals of Scripture become strangely beautiful.
Yet human failure could not stop God’s redemptive purpose.
That does not make their sins righteous.
Not another king with a divided heart.
Jesus does what every other human being in the story fails to do perfectly.
He goes willingly to the cross.
And there, the Gospel confronts every one of us.
God does not save you by pretending your scandal was never sinful.
He saves you by dealing with sin through Christ.
Jesus did not bleed so that we could learn better ways to excuse ourselves.
He died to reconcile sinners to God.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
It is the invitation to stop running from the One who already knows the truth.
The cross says your sin is serious enough that Christ had to die.
The resurrection says His grace is powerful enough that your sin does not have to write the final chapter.
Maybe your marriage has wounds nobody sees.
Maybe sexual sin has followed you for years.
Maybe you crossed lines you swore you never would.
Maybe you have wondered whether someone with your history can still become useful to God.
God never needed spotless human biographies to accomplish His purposes.
And everyone else comes needing grace.
“Abraham failed, so failure does not matter.”
“Abraham failed, David failed, Solomon failed, we fail—and we desperately need a Savior.”
Jesus does not merely edit the public version of your story.
And He calls forgiven people not merely to feel relieved…
So perhaps the real question after studying polygamy in the Old Testament is no longer:
“Why did God allow them to do that?”
What have I been asking God to tolerate in me that Jesus is calling me to surrender?
Because sometimes we become fascinated with somebody else’s scandal precisely because it keeps us from confronting our own.

And if Jesus has already brought you out of a chapter you thought would destroy you, tell somebody what His grace has done. Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded person needs tonight.
Not because an algorithm deserves your loyalty.
Because someone in your circle may be quietly wrestling with this exact question.
Someone may be using the failures of biblical characters as a reason to reject Scripture.
Someone may be using grace as permission to remain in sin.
Someone may believe their sexual or relational past has disqualified them permanently from Christ.
There are truths you understand differently when life finally makes them personal.
And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you understand Scripture, confront compromise, heal through biblical truth, and grow deeper in Jesus Christ, stay close to this ministry.
There is room here for difficult questions.
But every road must ultimately lead us back to Christ.
Not because Gospel Warrior can replace your local church, your responsibilities to your family, or Spirit-led generosity elsewhere.
Give because you have decided before God that this ministry is worth supporting.

Scripture teaches generosity freely given rather than extracted by pressure. Paul wrote that each person should give what he has decided in his heart, “not reluctantly or under compulsion” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
That is the spirit in which we ask.
Because the goal was never merely to win an argument about polygamy.
The goal is to read Scripture faithfully enough that eventually Scripture begins reading us.
Your religious reputation cannot save you.
And perhaps that is why God allowed the Bible to preserve so many uncomfortable stories.
If Scripture contained only flawless heroes, sinners like us might eventually imagine salvation belonged to flawless people.
Instead, page after page whispers the truth.
Human beings complicate what God made good.
And then Jesus enters the story.
The faithful One among the faithless.
The Bridegroom who does not abandon His bride.
The King whose heart never turns away from His Father.
The Savior who walks straight toward a cross carrying scandals that were never His.
So no—recording polygamy does not automatically mean God approved of it.
Sometimes the broken households of Scripture are not loopholes inviting us to lower God's design.
Sometimes they are warning lights showing us what happens when fallen humanity wanders from it.
And sometimes the darkest pages exist so that when grace finally appears in all its fullness, we understand just how desperately we needed it.
Your scandal may explain a chapter of your life—but once surrendered to Jesus Christ, it does not have the authority to write your ending.
